params.title: Transmitters
params.subtitle: How a transmitter makes, modulates and amplifies a radio signal: amplifier classes, FM and SSB, matching networks, clean signals.

onScreen: Amplifier classes, FM and SSB, matching networks and clean signals
scenes.narration: Welcome to Transmitters. A transmitter is the part of a radio that sends: it turns a voice or data into a strong, clean radio signal for the antenna, without spilling interference onto anyone else. As a technician, you'll test, tune and repair every stage. We'll build each idea from the ground up, assuming no background in electronics. By the end, you'll be able to name the amplifier classes and say why each is used. You'll work out the index and bandwidth of FM, frequency modulation, a transmitter's peak envelope power, and the voltage across a dummy load. And you'll see how single-sideband signals are made, how matching networks work, and how interference is kept out. First, a quick tour.

blocks.label: Oscillator
blocks.note: Makes the carrier: a steady radio wave

blocks.label: Modulator
blocks.note: Puts the voice or data on the carrier

blocks.label: Amplifiers
blocks.note: Build the signal up to full power

blocks.label: Matching network
blocks.note: Hands the power to the feed line

onScreen: Modulator: adds the voice or data
Matching network: feeds the line to the antenna
scenes.narration: Every transmitter does the same few jobs, in order. First comes an oscillator, a circuit that generates a steady radio wave called the carrier. The carrier is a smooth, repeating wave called a sine wave. Each repeat is a cycle, and the number of cycles each second is the frequency, measured in hertz: 1 hertz is 1 cycle per second. Next, a modulator puts the voice or data onto the carrier. Then amplifiers build the signal up to full power. Last, a matching network hands that power to the feed line, the cable that carries it to the antenna. We'll start with the amplifiers, where most of the exam questions are.

params.title: What an amplifier does
items: Like a tap on a water pipe: the DC supply is the pressure behind it
A small input controls a big flow; the extra power comes from the supply
Conducting: current flowing through the transistor or tube
Cutoff: fully off. Saturation: fully on. Linear region: in between
Bias: where the device rests with no signal

onScreen: Like a tap: the DC supply is the pressure
A small input controls a big flow from the supply
Conducting: current flows through the device
Cutoff, saturation and the linear region between
scenes.narration: So what does an amplifier actually do? Its working part, a transistor or a vacuum tube, acts like a tap on a water pipe. The power supply is the pressure behind the tap. It provides DC, direct current: a steady current that flows one way, like a battery's. The small input signal turns the handle, and a much bigger flow comes out that copies every turn; the extra power comes from the supply, not from the input. When current flows through the device, it is conducting. Close the tap fully and nothing flows: that's cutoff. Open it fully and no more can pass: that's saturation. In between is the linear region, where the output follows the input faithfully. Where the handle rests with no signal is the bias.

params.title: Class A: conducting for the whole cycle
labels: 1 cycle = 360°; each half = 180°
Conduction angle: the part of the cycle the device conducts
Class A: biased near the middle of the linear region
Input never reaches cutoff: output for the entire 360°

onScreen: Conduction angle: the part of the cycle the device conducts
Class A: biased near the middle of the linear region
scenes.narration: Now feed the amplifier a sine wave. We can measure a cycle in degrees, like one turn of a wheel: 1 full cycle is 360 degrees, and each half is 180 degrees. The conduction angle is the part of the cycle, in degrees, during which the device conducts. An amplifier's class is set by where its bias sits. A Class A amplifier is biased near the middle of its linear region. The input swings up and down around that point, but never far enough to go into cutoff. So the device conducts all the time, and output flows for the entire 360 degrees of the signal cycle. That's the distinguishing feature of Class A. The other classes all switch off for part of each cycle.

params.title: Class A: the most faithful copy
items: Linearity: the output is an exact, enlarged copy of the input
Distortion: any change in the wave's shape
The device's curve is straight in the middle and bends near cutoff and saturation
Class A stays on the straight part: highest linearity, least distortion

onScreen: The curve: straight in the middle
Class A: highest linearity, least distortion
scenes.narration: So a Class A amplifier never switches off, and that gives it its great strength: it makes the most faithful copy. Linearity means the output is an exact, enlarged copy of the input. Distortion is any change in the wave's shape. Plot the device's output against its input and you get a curve. Its middle part, the linear region, is straight, but it bends near cutoff and near saturation. A Class A amplifier stays on that straight part all the time. That's why, of all the classes, Class A has the highest linearity and the least distortion.

params.title: Voltage, current and resistance
rows: A part with a set resistance; makes heat

onScreen: Voltage E: the push, in volts
Current I: the flow, in amps
Resistance R: holds the flow back, in ohms
A resistor turns power into heat
scenes.narration: Class A sounds ideal, but it has a cost, and that cost is measured in power. So first, a quick refresher on electricity, using the water picture again. Voltage, written E, is the push, like water pressure, and it's measured in volts. Current, written I, is the flow, like the water moving through the pipe, measured in amperes, or amps. Resistance, written R, is whatever holds the flow back, like a narrow pipe, measured in ohms. A resistor is a part made to have a set resistance, and it turns the power it takes into heat.

params.title: Power: push times flow
steps: Current through a resistance: I = E ÷ R
Put that in place of I: P = E × (E ÷ R)

scenes.narration: Then there's power, written P: how fast energy is delivered, measured in watts. It's simply push times flow: P equals E times I. When a voltage pushes current through a resistance, the current is E divided by R: more push gives more flow, and more resistance gives less. Put E over R in place of I, and the power becomes E times E over R. E times E is E squared, so P equals E squared over R. That version needs only the voltage and the resistance, and we'll use it later to measure a transmitter's power.

params.title: Class A's price: efficiency
items: Efficiency: the share of DC input power that comes out as signal power
The rest turns into heat
Class A: no more than 50% efficient, even in theory
Why: it draws a steady current all the time, even with no signal

onScreen: Efficiency: signal power out ÷ DC power in
Class A: no more than 50%, even in theory
It draws current even with no signal
scenes.narration: With that, we can count Class A's cost. Efficiency is the share of the DC power going in that comes out as signal power; whatever doesn't come out as signal turns into heat. A Class A amplifier is no more than 50 percent efficient, even in theory. The reason is its bias in the middle of the linear region: the device draws a steady current all the time, even when there's no signal at all, and with no signal, every watt of it is spent as heat. Class A buys the most faithful copy with wasted power.

params.title: Class B: conducting for half the cycle
labels: Class B: biased exactly at cutoff
No signal: no current
Conducts on one half of the input wave: 180°

onScreen: Class B: biased exactly at cutoff
scenes.narration: To waste less power, move the bias down. A Class B amplifier is biased exactly at cutoff, right at the point where the device turns on. With no signal, it draws no current, so nothing is wasted while it waits. When the input swings up, the device turns on and conducts. When the input swings down, it is pushed further into cutoff and stays off. So Class B conducts for one half of the input wave: 180 degrees. On the exam, conduction for 180 degrees of the input wave means Class B, and Class B output is present for 180 degrees of the input cycle. The traps are 360 degrees, which is Class A, and less than 180, which is Class C.

Half a wave isn't much use on its own. The fix is to use 2 Class B devices in push-pull. The input is split into 2 opposite copies, one turned upside down, so the devices take turns. Device 1 conducts on one half of the cycle, for 180 degrees, while device 2 rests in cutoff. Then they swap, and device 2 conducts the other half. At the output the 2 halves are joined back together, and together they reproduce the complete waveform. One device pushes, the other pulls, which is where the name comes from. You'll meet push-pull again near the end of the lesson.

params.title: Class AB: a little more than half
labels: Class B's weak spot: a kink at the handover, crossover distortion
Class AB: bias between Class A and Class B, just above cutoff
Conducts a little even with no signal
Operating angle: more than 180° but less than 360°

onScreen: Class B's handover kink: crossover distortion
Class AB: bias between A and B
Conducts a little with no signal
scenes.narration: Class B push-pull has one weak spot. At the handover, as one device switches off and the other switches on, for a moment neither conducts properly, and the wave gets a small kink called crossover distortion. Class AB fixes this. Its bias sits between Class A and Class B, just above cutoff, so each device conducts a little even with no signal, and the handover is smooth. Driven by a sine wave, each device conducts for more than half of each cycle, but still cuts off for part of it. Here the exam calls the conduction angle the operating angle. Class AB has an operating angle of more than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees, and its output is present for that portion of the input cycle.

params.title: Class C: conducting only on the peaks
labels: Class C: bias set well beyond cutoff
Only the peaks of the drive make it conduct
Output for less than 180° of the cycle

onScreen: Class C: bias well beyond cutoff
Only the drive peaks make it conduct
scenes.narration: Now go the other way, past Class B. A Class C amplifier's bias is set well beyond cutoff, so the device rests switched off with room to spare. The input has to climb a long way before the device turns on, and only the peaks of the drive, the input signal, climb that far. So Class C conducts, and its output is present, for less than 180 degrees of the input cycle. Remember the difference: Class B is biased right at cutoff and conducts for exactly half; Class C is biased well beyond cutoff and conducts for less than half. What comes out is a string of short pulses, one per cycle.

params.title: The tank circuit restores the sine wave

blocks.label: Tuned output tank circuit
blocks.note: A coil and a capacitor tuned to the carrier

onScreen: Tuned output tank circuit: a coil and a capacitor
scenes.narration: So how do those short pulses from the Class C device become a clean carrier? Think of a child on a swing. You don't have to push a swing all the way round; a short push at the right moment keeps it swinging smoothly. In a transmitter, the swing is a tuned output tank circuit. It's a coil of wire, called an inductor, connected to a capacitor, a pair of metal plates that stores electric charge. Energy sloshes back and forth between them at one natural frequency, and tuned means that frequency is set to match the carrier. Each pulse tops up the tank, and the tank rings on through the rest of the cycle, restoring a complete sine wave at the output.

params.title: Class A versus Class C
rows: No more than 50%, even in theory
Cut off for most of each cycle
Low: the pulses lose the input's shape

onScreen: Class C: cut off for most of each cycle
scenes.narration: So Class C can still deliver a clean carrier. Why go to that trouble? Because Class C is the efficiency champion. It provides the highest efficiency of these classes, around 70 to 80 percent, compared with no more than 50 percent for Class A. That's because its device is cut off for most of each cycle, so it wastes little power as heat. The cost is linearity. The pulses look nothing like the input, so any rise and fall in the input's strength is lost. The 2 classes sit at opposite ends: Class A is the most linear and the least efficient, and Class C is the reverse.

params.title: Where Class C works, and where it doesn't
items: Class C suits signals whose strength carries no message
SSB, single sideband: strength rises and falls with speech, so too nonlinear
CW, continuous wave: Morse code, a steady carrier switched on and off
FM, frequency modulation: the voice changes the frequency, not the strength
CW and FM keep a constant strength: Class C works well for both

onScreen: Class C suits signals of constant strength
CW: a steady carrier, on or off
FM: the frequency changes, not the strength
Class C works well for CW and FM
scenes.narration: Where, then, can Class C be used? Anywhere the signal's strength doesn't carry the message. SSB, single sideband, is a voice mode whose strength rises and falls with the speech. Class C would lose those changes, so it's too nonlinear for SSB. CW, continuous wave, is Morse code sent by switching a steady carrier on and off. FM, frequency modulation, which we'll meet properly later, carries the voice in small changes of the carrier's frequency, not its strength. In CW and FM the strength stays constant, so there's nothing for Class C to spoil, and it works well for both.

params.title: Conduction angle by class
rows: Near the middle of the linear region
Between Class A and Class B

onScreen: Class AB: more than 180°, less than 360°
scenes.narration: That completes the 4 classes. The exam's answer choices are their 4 conduction angles, so let's line them up. Class A, biased near the middle of its linear region: output for the entire 360 degrees. Class AB, biased between A and B: more than 180 but less than 360 degrees. Class B, biased exactly at cutoff: 180 degrees, half the wave. Class C, biased well beyond cutoff: less than 180 degrees. Going down the table, the bias moves down to cutoff and beyond, the conduction angle shrinks and the efficiency climbs, while the linearity falls. Remember the order: 360, more than 180, exactly 180, and less than 180.

params.title: Measuring a wave's size
labels: Peak: from the center line to the top
Peak-to-peak: from the bottom to the top, twice the peak
RMS: 0.707 × peak, the heating value
Average over a half cycle: lower still

scenes.narration: Back to Class A for one more exam question, about signal size. First, the ways of stating how big a wave is. The peak is the height from the center line to the top of the wave. Peak-to-peak is from the very bottom to the very top, so it's twice the peak. Then there are values that smooth the wave out. The RMS, or root mean square, value is the steady DC voltage that would heat a resistor just as much; for a sine wave, it's 0.707 times the peak. The average value, the wave's average height over a half cycle, is lower still. Meters usually show these smoothed values, but an amplifier feels every peak.

params.title: Judging a Class A amplifier's input
items: Class A stays linear only between cutoff and saturation
Peaks that reach cutoff or saturation are clipped flat
Average or RMS values can hide those peaks
Most valuable input-amplitude parameter: the peak voltage
Resting voltage: just the bias, with no signal

onScreen: Linear only between cutoff and saturation
Peaks that reach either are clipped
Average or RMS can hide the peaks
scenes.narration: So how do you judge how big a signal a Class A amplifier can handle? Remember, Class A stays linear only between cutoff and saturation. If the input's peaks reach either one, the output is clipped: the top or bottom of the wave is sliced flat, and that's distortion. An average or RMS value can look perfectly safe while hiding peaks that go too far. So, of all the input-amplitude parameters, the most valuable for evaluating a Class A amplifier's signal-handling capability is the peak voltage. The traps are average, RMS and resting voltage. The resting voltage is just the bias, with no signal at all, so it tells you nothing about the peaks.

params.title: DC input power for a Class AB amplifier
steps: Efficiency = output ÷ DC input, turned around
Class AB RF linear amplifier: about 50%, or 0.5

onScreen: Efficiency = output ÷ DC input, turned around
scenes.narration: The last amplifier question: how much power does an amplifier draw from its supply? Efficiency is the output power divided by the DC input power. Turn that around, and the DC input power is the output power divided by the efficiency. A Class AB linear amplifier for RF, meaning radio frequency signals, is roughly 50 percent efficient. The exam's case: a Class AB RF power amplifier delivers 500 watts PEP, peak envelope power, its output at the signal's strongest moment. 50 percent as a decimal is 0.5, so the DC input is 500 watts divided by 0.5: 1,000 watts. Does that make sense? At 50 percent, half the input becomes output, so the input must be twice the output. Multiplying instead gives the 250 watt trap.

params.title: Modulation: putting information on the carrier

scenes.narration: That's the amplifier side. But amplifiers only boost what they're given; the message goes on earlier in the chain, at the modulator. A plain carrier holds no message; modulation means varying the carrier in step with the voice or data. There are 3 basic ways. AM, amplitude modulation, varies the carrier's strength, its amplitude. FM varies its frequency: the carrier runs a little faster, then a little slower. And PM, phase modulation, varies its phase. Phase means where a wave is in its cycle, in degrees, so PM nudges the carrier's timing a little ahead of or behind where it would otherwise be. FM and PM are close cousins, and both keep the carrier's strength constant.

params.title: FM: deviation and modulating frequency
labels: Modulating frequency: how often the sound swings the carrier
Deviation: how far the carrier's frequency swings
Louder sound: more deviation
Higher pitch: a higher modulating frequency

onScreen: Modulating frequency: how often it swings
scenes.narration: Let's look closer at FM. 2 numbers describe it. The modulating frequency is the frequency of the sound being sent: a 1,000 hertz tone swings the carrier back and forth 1,000 times a second. The deviation is how far the carrier's frequency swings away from its resting value on each side, also measured in hertz, or in kilohertz, where 1 kilohertz is 1,000 hertz. A louder sound gives more deviation, and a higher-pitched sound gives a higher modulating frequency. On screen, the wave bunches up where its frequency swings up and spreads out where it swings down.

params.title: FM modulation index
steps: Deviation: 3,000 Hz on either side of the carrier

scenes.narration: Those 2 numbers combine into the FM modulation index, m: the frequency deviation divided by the modulating frequency. It compares how far the carrier swings with how fast the swinging happens. Take the exam's example: a maximum deviation of 3,000 hertz on either side of the carrier, with a 1,000 hertz modulating frequency. Divide the deviation by the modulating frequency: 3,000 hertz over 1,000 hertz is 3. So the modulation index is 3: the swing is 3 times the tone's own frequency. The traps 3,000 and 1,000 just repeat the starting numbers, and 0.3 is off by a factor of 10.

params.title: The index is a plain number
params.answer: m = 3: a ratio, with no units

scenes.narration: Here's the second example: a maximum carrier deviation of 6 kilohertz, with a 2 kilohertz modulating frequency. Notice what happens to the units. Kilohertz divided by kilohertz cancel out, just as dividing meters by meters leaves no meters. 6 divided by 2 is 3, so the index is again 3. The modulation index is a ratio: a plain number with no units. That also exposes the traps: 6,000 and 2,000 are just the starting numbers written in hertz, and 1 would mean the swing equals the tone's frequency.

params.title: Carson's rule for FM bandwidth
steps: Deviation: the carrier's swing to 1 side
Plus about 1 modulating frequency of spread
Double it, for both sides: 2 × 8 kHz

onScreen: Deviation plus 1 modulating frequency, each side
scenes.narration: Deviation and the modulating frequency also decide an FM signal's bandwidth: the slice of frequencies it occupies, like the width of a lane on a highway. Carson's rule estimates it as twice the sum of the deviation and the highest modulating frequency. Why? On each side, the carrier swings out by the deviation, and the modulation spreads the signal about 1 modulating frequency further. So with 5 kilohertz of deviation and a 3 kilohertz modulating frequency, one side takes 5 plus 3: 8 kilohertz. Double it to cover both sides of the carrier: 16 kilohertz. The trap of 8 kilohertz is what you get if you forget to double.

params.title: Phase modulation index
labels: PM index: the peak phase shift of the carrier
Set by the amplitude of the modulating signal
Does not depend on the RF carrier frequency

onScreen: Set by the modulating signal's amplitude
Independent of the RF carrier frequency
scenes.narration: FM's close cousin, phase modulation, has a modulation index too. For a phase-modulated emission, the index is the peak phase shift: the furthest the carrier's timing is nudged ahead or behind. That shift is set by the amplitude, the strength, of the modulating signal: louder audio, bigger shift. So how does the index vary with the RF carrier frequency? It doesn't. The shift depends on how hard the audio pushes, not on how fast the carrier runs. The same audio gives the same index whether the carrier is at 2 megahertz or 450 megahertz, where 1 megahertz is 1,000 kilohertz. The traps say it rises, falls, or follows the square root of the carrier frequency.

params.title: Sidebands: where the voice really goes
labels: Frequency runs across: each signal is a spike
Mixing makes sum and difference frequencies: the sidebands
Upper: carrier + audio, the sum. Lower: carrier − audio
Carrier: none of the voice. Each sideband: all of it

onScreen: Frequency across: each signal a spike
Upper sideband: the sum; lower: the difference
The carrier carries none of the voice; each sideband carries all of it
scenes.narration: The rest of the modulation questions are about single sideband, which grows out of AM. This picture plots frequency, not time: each signal shows as a spike at its own frequency. Varying a carrier's strength with audio is a kind of mixing: in effect it multiplies the 2 signals, which always makes 2 new frequencies, their sum and their difference, called sidebands. The upper sideband is the carrier plus the audio frequency: the sum. The lower one is the carrier minus the audio: the difference. Now the surprise. The carrier stays the same whatever is said, so it carries none of the voice, while each sideband carries all of it. That's why single sideband sends just 1 sideband, with no carrier.

blocks.label: Balanced modulator
blocks.note: The carrier cancels; the sidebands pass

blocks.label: DSB, suppressed carrier
blocks.note: Double sideband: both sidebands, no carrier

scenes.narration: The first step toward single sideband is to get rid of the carrier. That's the job of a balanced modulator. Audio from the microphone and a signal from the carrier oscillator both feed into it. Inside are 2 matching halves, arranged so the carrier comes out of one half exactly opposite to the other, and the 2 cancel, like 2 equal pushes in opposite directions. The sum and difference sidebands come out in step, so they pass through. The result is a double sideband, or DSB, suppressed carrier signal. That's the exam's definition: a balanced modulator is a modulator that produces a double sideband, suppressed carrier signal. The traps call it single sideband or full carrier, but it is neither.

From double sideband, one more step gives single sideband. After the balanced modulator comes a sharp filter that lets one sideband through and removes the unwanted one. What's left is a single-sideband phone signal, phone meaning voice. So a single-sideband phone signal is generated by a balanced modulator followed by a filter. The trap answers borrow parts from elsewhere: a product detector is a receiver part, and the reactance modulator in another trap is a way of making FM.

params.title: Single sideband, suppressed carrier
labels: Cancel the carrier: in a balanced modulator
Filter the unwanted sideband: a crystal or mechanical filter
What remains: 1 sideband, no carrier

onScreen: Filter the unwanted sideband: crystal or mechanical filter
scenes.narration: That's how SSB is made. Now let's look at the SSB transmitter as a whole, starting with the exam's fill-in-the-blank: to produce single sideband, suppressed carrier, you cancel the carrier and filter the unwanted sideband. The carrier is canceled in the balanced modulator. The unwanted sideband is then filtered out, usually by a crystal filter, which uses slices of quartz that vibrate at precise frequencies, or by a mechanical filter, which uses tiny vibrating metal parts. The filter must be very sharp, because the 2 sidebands sit close together on either side of where the carrier was. Cancel, then filter: the traps swap or repeat those 2 words.

blocks.label: Linear amplifier
blocks.note: Class A or AB: keeps the shape

blocks.label: Non-linear amplifier
blocks.note: Such as Class C: bends the envelope

scenes.narration: Next, the SSB signal has to be amplified, and here the amplifier classes come back. The outline of a signal's strength over time is called its envelope. An SSB signal has no carrier, so its envelope follows the speech, rising and falling with your voice. To keep that shape, every amplifier after the filter must be linear, such as Class A or Class AB. So what happens if you use a non-linear amplifier, such as Class C, with a single-sideband phone transmitter? Distortion. The bent envelope creates intermodulation products, new unwanted frequencies made when parts of the signal mix together, and splatter, which spreads the signal into neighboring channels. Reduced efficiency, better intelligibility and sideband inversion are the traps.

params.title: Peak and average power in SSB voice
labels: PEP: the power at the envelope's highest point
Average power: the power averaged over time
No carrier: the output follows the voice
Speech characteristics set the PEP-to-average ratio

onScreen: PEP: power at the envelope's peak
No carrier: output follows the voice
scenes.narration: Because the SSB envelope follows the voice, its power isn't steady, so we describe it with 2 numbers. You met PEP, peak envelope power, in the amplifier calculation; now we can say exactly what it is: the power at the very highest point of the envelope. Average power is the power averaged over time, quiet moments included. In an SSB phone signal there's no carrier, so between words the output falls to almost nothing. That means the ratio of PEP to average power is set by the speech characteristics of the talker: how often they pause, how they stress words, the quality of their voice. The traps, the modulating frequency, the degree of carrier suppression and the amplifier power, don't set it.

params.title: The 2.5 to 1 ratio
items: Speech: strong peaks between quieter stretches and pauses
Normal voice peaks: PEP about 2.5 times the average power
PEP-to-average ratio: approximately 2.5 to 1
Traps: 1 to 1 (a steady carrier), 25 to 1, 100 to 1

scenes.narration: So what's a typical figure? Speech has strong peaks separated by quieter stretches and pauses. During normal voice modulation peaks, the peak envelope power in an SSB phone signal is about 2.5 times the average power. In other words, the PEP-to-average power ratio is approximately 2.5 to 1. A ratio of 1 to 1 would mean a perfectly steady signal, like a plain carrier, while 25 to 1 and 100 to 1 are far too high for normal speech. The exact ratio varies with the voice and any speech processing, but for the exam, remember 2.5 to 1.

Now let's measure PEP on a real transmitter, using an oscilloscope, an instrument that draws a voltage as a wave on its screen. Say the scope, connected across a 50-ohm load resistor, shows 200 volts peak-to-peak. Power needs the RMS voltage, E sub r-m-s, the heating value from earlier, so convert the reading in 2 steps. First, halve the peak-to-peak to get the peak: 200 divided by 2 is 100 volts. Then multiply the peak by 0.707 to get RMS: 100 times 0.707 is 70.7 volts.

With the RMS voltage in hand, use the power formula from earlier: PEP equals E sub r-m-s squared over R, where R is the load resistance in ohms. The scope showed the tallest swing of the envelope, so the power we get is the power at the envelope's peak. Square 70.7 volts: 70.7 times 70.7 is about 5,000. Divide by the 50-ohm load: 5,000 over 50 is 100 watts. So the PEP is 100 watts. A common slip is to skip the 0.707 step and square the 100-volt peak instead: 100 squared over 50 gives 200 watts, one of the trap answers.

params.title: Voltage across a dummy load
params.formula: P = E² ÷ R, so E = √(P × R)
steps: Dummy load: R = 50 Ω, P = 1,200 W

scenes.narration: One more power calculation. A dummy load is a big resistor that stands in for the antenna during testing: it soaks up the transmitter's power as heat instead of sending it over the air. What voltage appears across a 50-ohm dummy load dissipating 1,200 watts? Start from P equals E squared over R, and turn it around. Multiply both sides by R: E squared equals P times R. Then take the square root: E equals the square root of P times R. So E is the square root of 1,200 times 50, the square root of 60,000, which is about 245 volts. Check: 245 squared is about 60,000, and 60,000 over 50 is 1,200 watts.

params.title: Matching the amplifier to the line

blocks.label: Matching network
blocks.note: Transforms one impedance to the other

scenes.narration: A dummy load is a simple resistor, but a real amplifier and a real antenna system aren't so easy to join. The reason is impedance: the total opposition a circuit offers to alternating current, or AC, the back-and-forth current of a radio signal, measured in ohms. The amplifying device has its own output impedance. The matching network after it transforms that impedance into the one the feed line needs, the way a bicycle's gears match your legs to the wheel. The feed line, also called the transmission line, has its own impedance, often 50 ohms, and carries the power on to the antenna. Without the match, power is reflected or wasted instead of delivered. Matching networks are built from coils and capacitors, so let's see how those behave.

params.title: Coils, capacitors and reactance
rows: Its plates fill up and push back
Store energy and give it back

onScreen: Reactance: in ohms, stores energy, makes no heat
scenes.narration: You met the coil and the capacitor in the tank circuit. Here's how each one opposes AC. The inductor, our coil of wire, resists any change in the current through it. The faster the current reverses, the harder it pushes back, so its opposition, called inductive reactance, X sub L, rises as the frequency rises. The capacitor's 2 metal plates are separated by an insulator, and its opposition, capacitive reactance, X sub C, does the opposite: it falls as the frequency rises, because at high frequency the plates have less time to fill up and push back. Reactance is measured in ohms, like resistance, but it stores energy and gives it back instead of turning it into heat.

params.title: Resonance
steps: X<sub>L</sub> rises with frequency; X<sub>C</sub> falls
At one frequency they are equal
They cancel: a purely resistive circuit

scenes.narration: Put the 2 together, and one reactance rises with frequency while the other falls, so there's exactly one frequency where they're equal. That's the resonant frequency: the frequency at which capacitive reactance equals inductive reactance, X sub L equals X sub C. There, the 2 reactances push in opposite directions and cancel, leaving a purely resistive circuit, one that acts like a plain resistance. It's the frequency at which a tank circuit naturally rings. Solving for it gives f equals 1 over the quantity 2 pi times the square root of L times C, where L and C are the sizes of the coil and the capacitor. Bigger parts mean a lower frequency. The traps, the highest or lowest frequency that passes current, don't describe resonance.

params.title: The L network
items: Series: in the signal's path
Shunt: from the path down to ground
L network: 1 inductor and 1 capacitor
One in series, the other shunted to ground
The schematic looks like the letter L

onScreen: Shunt: from the path to ground
One in series, one shunted to ground
scenes.narration: With coils and capacitors understood, we can build the 3 matching networks. First, 2 words for how a part is connected. A part in series sits in the signal's path, so the signal passes through it. A part in shunt connects from the path down to ground, the circuit's common return at zero volts, giving the signal a side route. The simplest network is the L network: an inductor and a capacitor, one in series and the other shunted to ground. Drawn on a schematic, the series part runs across and the shunt part drops down, so it looks like the letter L. The traps, a Wi-Fi connection, a lossy network or 2 filters joined together, are word games.

params.title: The pi network
items: 1 series element between 2 shunt elements
Shaped like the Greek letter π
1 inductor and 2 capacitors, or 2 inductors and 1 capacitor
In transmitters: usually 2 capacitors to ground, a coil between

onScreen: 1 inductor and 2 capacitors, or 2 inductors and 1 capacitor
scenes.narration: Add a third part and you get a pi network. It has 1 series element between 2 shunt elements: a shunt part at the input, a series part across the top, and a shunt part at the output. Drawn out, the 2 shunt legs hang down from the series bar like the Greek letter pi. A pi network consists of 1 inductor and 2 capacitors, or 2 inductors and 1 capacitor. In transmitters, it's usually 2 capacitors to ground with an inductor between them. The trap answers, a capacitor, resistor and inductor, a phase inversion stage, or a token ring network, don't fit that shape.

params.title: The pi-L network
items: A pi network followed by a second series inductor
The L section shares the pi's output capacitor
Total: 2 inductors and 2 capacitors
Traps: only 3 parts (a plain pi), or every part isolated from ground

onScreen: A pi network plus a series inductor
Traps: 3 parts, or isolated from ground
scenes.narration: Now extend the pi. A pi-L network is a pi network, capacitor, inductor, capacitor, followed by a second series inductor. That extra inductor and the pi's output capacitor together make an L section, so the output capacitor is shared by both. Count the parts: 2 inductors and 2 capacitors. That's the exam's answer to what a pi-L network is. The traps say 3 parts, which is a plain pi, or a network with every part isolated from ground, which can't be right, since its capacitors are shunted to ground.

onScreen: Harmonics at 2, 3 and 4 times the carrier
Made when an amplifier bends the wave
scenes.narration: Matching networks have a second job, and it starts with a problem. Any amplifier that bends the wave, Class C most of all, creates harmonics: extra signals at whole-number multiples of the carrier frequency, f. The first of them, the 2nd harmonic, sits at 2 times f. Why do they appear at all? A pure sine wave has no harmonics, but any other repeating shape, such as a pulse or a clipped wave, is really a sine wave plus a set of harmonics. So a bent wave also carries a 3rd harmonic, at 3 times f, a 4th, at 4 times f, and so on. If they reached the antenna, they'd interfere with stations far up the band, so they have to be stopped.

params.title: Matching networks are low-pass filters
items: Low-pass filter: passes frequencies below a chosen point, blocks those above
Series coil: its reactance rises with frequency, so it holds harmonics back
Shunt capacitor: its reactance falls with frequency, so harmonics go to ground
L, pi and pi-L: the 3 networks that match an amplifying device to a transmission line
Each also acts as a low-pass filter

onScreen: Low-pass: passes low frequencies, blocks high ones
Shunt capacitor sends them to ground
L, pi and pi-L networks match a device to a line
Each is also a low-pass filter
scenes.narration: What stops them is a low-pass filter: a circuit that passes frequencies below a chosen point and blocks those above it, so it lets the carrier through and stops its harmonics. Here's the useful part: a matching network built the usual way already is one. Its series coil has a reactance that rises with frequency, so it holds the harmonics back. The capacitors shunted to ground have a reactance that falls with frequency, so the harmonics slip away to ground. That's why the 3 network types commonly used to match an amplifying device to a transmission line, the L network, the pi network and the pi-L network, each also act as a low-pass filter. The traps list T, M, Z and C networks.

params.title: Which network suppresses harmonics best?
rows: The greatest: an extra low-pass L section

scenes.narration: So which network provides the greatest harmonic suppression? Start with the simplest. The L network has 1 coil and 1 capacitor: a single low-pass section. Think of each low-pass section as a sieve that holds back some of the harmonics. The pi network has 3 parts. The pi-L network goes further: it adds an extra low-pass L section on the end of the pi, so the harmonics pass through more filtering before they reach the antenna. That gives the pi-L the greatest harmonic suppression, more than a simple L or pi network, and the inverse L trap is no better. The takeaway: L, pi and pi-L networks all match and filter, and the pi-L filters best.

onScreen: Even-order harmonics: 2, 4 or 6 times the carrier
Push-pull reduces or prevents the even ones
scenes.narration: That's matching and filtering. The rest of the lesson keeps the signal clean in other ways, and the first one stops some harmonics before they're even made. Harmonics come in 2 kinds. Even-order harmonics fall at even multiples of the carrier: 2 times, 4 times, 6 times. Odd-order harmonics fall at odd multiples: 3, 5 or 7 times. Even-order harmonics are reduced or prevented by a push-pull amplifier, the layout we met with Class B, where 2 devices take turns on opposite halves of the wave. That's the exam's answer. Now let's see why it works.

blocks.label: Device 2
blocks.note: Its even harmonics in step with device 1's

onScreen: Their even harmonics come out in step
The center-tapped transformer passes the difference
scenes.narration: The trick is in the timing. The 2 devices are driven 180 degrees out of phase, half a cycle apart, so each gets an upside-down copy of the other's input. The second harmonic runs at twice the carrier frequency, so half a carrier cycle is one whole cycle of it. After that half-cycle delay, the second harmonics from the 2 devices are exactly in step, and so is every even harmonic. The devices feed the 2 ends of a center-tapped output transformer: 2 coils wound together, the first one tapped in its middle. It passes on only the difference between its 2 halves. The difference of 2 opposite signals is double; the difference of 2 matching ones is nothing. So the wanted signal comes through, and the even-harmonic currents cancel.

Don't confuse push-pull with push-push. A push-push stage drives its 2 devices out of phase too, but joins their outputs together instead of feeding opposite ends of the transformer. Now it's the sum that comes out: the wanted signal, opposite in the 2 devices, cancels, while the even harmonics, in step, add up. The strongest is the second harmonic, at twice the input frequency. So push-push reinforces even harmonics instead of canceling them, which is why it's used as a frequency doubler. On the exam, preventing even-order harmonics means push-pull. Push-push, Class C and Class AB are the traps.

blocks.label: Our antenna and feed line
blocks.note: Carry its signal back to our final

onScreen: Travels back down our feed line
scenes.narration: Harmonics come from inside our own transmitter. Interference can also come from a neighbor. When 2 transmitters are in close proximity, say on the same mast or the same ship, each antenna picks up some of the other's signal. That signal travels backward down the feed line into the final amplifier, the last and most powerful stage. No final amplifier is perfectly linear, so it mixes the 2 signals together, and, just as in a modulator, mixing creates new signals at the sum and difference of the original frequencies. When the signals of 2 nearby transmitters mix in one or both of their final amplifiers like this, the condition is called intermodulation interference. The traps are amplifier desensitization, neutralization and adjacent channel interference.

blocks.label: Circulator
blocks.note: Ferrite: power goes round one way only

blocks.label: Load
blocks.note: Absorbs power from the antenna side

onScreen: A circulator in the feed line
Our signal goes round to the antenna
Power from the antenna side goes into a load
scenes.narration: The cure is to keep the neighbor's signal out of our final amplifier, with a one-way device in the feed line. A circulator works like a one-way traffic circle. It's built around ferrite, a magnetic ceramic, and power can only travel round it in one direction. Power from our transmitter goes round to the antenna. But power arriving from the antenna side, including the neighbor's signal, carries on round into a load, a resistor that soaks it up as heat. Terminated means that load is fitted. A ferrite isolator does the same job in a single package.

params.title: Intermodulation: the exam's cure
items: Install a terminated circulator or ferrite isolator
In the feed line to the transmitter and duplexer
Duplexer: lets a transmitter and a receiver share one antenna
Trap: low-pass or band-pass filters: the other signal can pass them
Trap: a Class C final with high drive: it would only mix harder

onScreen: In the feed line to the transmitter and duplexer
Class C with high drive is a trap
scenes.narration: So, for the exam: intermodulation between 2 transmitters in close proximity can often be reduced or eliminated by installing a terminated circulator or ferrite isolator in the feed line to the transmitter and duplexer. A duplexer is the unit that lets a transmitter and a receiver share one antenna. The traps offer filters instead. A low-pass or band-pass filter in the feed line won't help, because the other signal is often close enough in frequency to pass straight through it. And a Class C final amplifier with high driving power, the last trap, is very nonlinear, so it would only mix harder.

blocks.label: Internal capacitance
blocks.note: A tiny capacitor inside the device

onScreen: Output leaks back through internal capacitance
scenes.narration: One problem is left, and it starts inside the amplifier itself. In every transistor or tube, the input and output parts sit close together, like the plates of a tiny capacitor. This is its internal capacitance, and through it some of the output leaks back to the input. If that leaked signal arrives in step with the input, the amplifier amplifies it again, and again, and keeps itself going even with no input. That's an oscillation: what an oscillator does on purpose, or the howl when a microphone gets too close to its speaker. When it happens by accident, at unwanted frequencies, it's called a parasitic oscillation.

params.title: Stopping parasitic oscillations
items: Parasitic oscillations in a power amplifier are eliminated by neutralization
Neutralization feeds back an equal signal of opposite phase
It cancels the coupling through the device's internal capacitance
Tuning for maximum output or SWR does not remove that feedback path

onScreen: An equal signal of opposite phase is fed back
Tuning for output or SWR doesn't remove it
scenes.narration: So how are parasitic oscillations eliminated in a power amplifier? By neutralization. A neutralizing circuit deliberately feeds a second signal from the output back to the input, equal in size to the leak but opposite in phase. The 2 cancel at the input, so the coupling through the device's internal capacitance no longer feeds anything back. The traps are all about tuning: tuning for maximum power output, for maximum SWR, standing wave ratio, a measure of how badly the line is mismatched, or just tuning the output. Tuning adjusts the output network, but it doesn't touch the feedback path inside the device, so it won't cure parasitics.

onScreen: Spread spectrum: the carrier hops in a pre-determined sequence
scenes.narration: Our last topic isn't a problem but a different way to use the band. Most signals, including SSB and FM, each stay on 1 fixed carrier frequency. Spread spectrum doesn't. It's a wide-bandwidth communication system in which the RF carrier varies according to a pre-determined sequence, a pattern known to both the sender and the receiver, so the receiver can hop along in step. Because the signal never stays long on one frequency, it's hard to jam or interfere with. Spread spectrum is also the modulation type that can be a frequency hopping of 1 carrier, or of multiple simultaneous carriers. Don't confuse it with AMTOR, amateur teleprinting over radio, or SITOR, simplex teleprinting over radio: narrow-band modes that send text on a single small channel.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: Class A 360°, AB more than 180°, B 180°, C less than 180°
Class A: most linear, no more than 50% efficient. Class C: 70 to 80%
FM index = deviation ÷ modulating frequency; Carson: 2 × (dev. + mod. freq.)
SSB: balanced modulator, then filter; amplify linearly; PEP ≈ 2.5 × average
Pi-L filters best; push-pull cancels even harmonics; neutralization stops parasitics

onScreen: Conduction: A 360°, AB more than 180°, B 180°, C less than 180°
Class A most linear; Class C most efficient
SSB: balanced modulator and filter, linear amplifiers, 2.5 to 1
scenes.narration: That's the whole transmitter, from oscillator to antenna. Here's what to remember. Class A conducts for 360 degrees, AB for more than 180, B for exactly 180, and C for less than 180. Class A is the most linear but no more than 50 percent efficient; Class C reaches 70 to 80 percent but is too nonlinear for SSB. The FM index is deviation divided by modulating frequency, and Carson's rule doubles their sum for bandwidth. Single sideband comes from a balanced modulator and a filter, must be amplified linearly, and peaks at about 2.5 times its average power. And to keep the signal clean, the pi-L network filters harmonics best, push-pull cancels the even ones, and neutralization stops parasitic oscillations.
